result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.immediate_dominators()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the immediate dominator of every node reachable from a start node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45541-L45618){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.immediate_dominators(start) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Immediate dominators](/assets/graphs/immediate-dominators.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="An if/else control-flow graph: entry (outlined) leads to if, which branches to then and else; both rejoin at merge, which leads to exit. The dominator tree is drawn in the accent color: every path to merge passes through if but through neither branch, so the dashed accent arrow if to merge replaces the faded branch edges. The card maps each node to its immediate dominator: if for then, else and merge, merge for exit." width="100%"} In a directed graph with a start node, a node `d` *dominates* node `v` if every path from the start to `v` passes through `d`. The *immediate* dominator of `v` is its closest strict dominator, and linking every node to it forms the dominator tree. Dominators come from compiler design (control-flow analysis, loop detection, placing code), and in networks they identify single points of failure: a node's immediate dominator is the last unavoidable relay on the way from a source, such as a router every packet to a host must traverse, or a gene that every regulatory path to another passes through. Only nodes reachable from `start` appear in the result, and `start` maps to itself. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [start]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The start (entry) node, as an ID or label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : For every reachable node ID, the ID of its immediate dominator. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or `start` does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} This is the iterative algorithm of Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy (2001), as in NetworkX: nodes are processed in reverse postorder of a depth-first search, each node's dominator is updated to the nearest common dominator of its processed predecessors, and the pass repeats until nothing changes. It is simple and fast in practice, $O(V^2)$ in the worst case. Dominance frontiers follow from the dominator tree; see `dominance_frontiers()`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a small control-flow graph, both branches of an if/else rejoin at `merge`, so the immediate dominator of `merge` is `if`, not either branch: ::: {#93da9a06 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["entry", "if", "then", "else", "merge", "exit"]) g.add_edges( [ ("entry", "if"), ("if", "then"), ("if", "else"), ("then", "merge"), ("else", "merge"), ("merge", "exit"), ] ) idom = g.immediate_dominators("entry") {g.get_label_from_id(n): g.get_label_from_id(d) for n, d in idom.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'entry': 'entry', 'if': 'entry', 'then': 'if', 'else': 'if', 'merge': 'if', 'exit': 'merge'} ``` ::: :::
